name: Uriah the Hittite
charge: The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; shall I then go into mine house? as thou livest, I will not do this thing
summary: One of David’s mighty men, recalled from the siege of Rabbah so that the king’s sin could be covered. He would not go down to his house, but slept at the door of the king’s house with the servants of his lord; asked why, he answered that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents and Joab and the servants were encamped in the open fields, and swore he would not do this thing. Made drunk, he still would not go, and was sent back carrying the letter that ordered his death. The king could command his movements, but he could not make the blood innocent: Nathan named him, and the record of the kings and the ancestry of Christ still name him.
offenseFull: David sent to Joab for Uriah the Hittite, and when he came the king asked him how Joab did and how the people did and how the war prospered, and then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, and a mess of meat from the king followed him; but Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord and went not down to his house (2 Samuel 11:6-9). Uriah was no ordinary soldier; he is numbered among the thirty and seven mighty men of David (2 Samuel 23:39), one of the men Joab had at the front, and the small talk from the king was out of the ordinary for him. The name Hittite does not make him a Hamite in David’s army; men in that record carry the names of the lands they dwelt in after Israel removed the nations from those coasts. When David was told that he had not gone down, he asked why, since he had come from a journey, he went not down to his house; and Uriah answered that the ark, and Israel, and Judah abode in tents, and his lord Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields, so how could he go into his house to eat and to drink and to lie with his wife, and he swore by the king’s life that he would not do this thing (2 Samuel 11:6-11; 2 Samuel 11:10-11). He remembered the men still carrying the burden he had been briefly recalled from, and he remembered the ark in a tent. David kept him there another day, called him to eat and drink before him and made him drunk, and at evening he went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house (2 Samuel 11:12-13). Even drunk, when a man might just go home and sleep it off, he would not go. That loyalty was killing David all

the more, because he could not deceive this man into lying with his own wife. In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that he be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and that they retire from him, that he might be smitten and die (2 Samuel 11:14-17; 2 Samuel 11:14-15). He carried his own death warrant to the captain without opening it. Joab assigned him to a place where he knew valiant men were, the men of the city came out and fought, some of the servants of David fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also (2 Samuel 11:16-17). His death exposed no failure of duty in him; it exposed the treachery of the command set over him.
judgmentFull: The king tried to hide him among the ordinary losses of war, saying the sword devoureth one as well as another (2 Samuel 11:25), and Joab knew what the king really wanted and charged the messenger to name Uriah the Hittite as dead also (2 Samuel 11:21-25; 2 Samuel 11:21-24). The Lord did not let him disappear in the casualty list. Nathan named him to his face in the judgment on the king: David had killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword and taken his wife to be his wife, and slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon (2 Samuel 12:9). The curse that fell was the curse written for the man who did it: a curse lies on the man who strikes his neighbour in secret and on the man who takes a reward to kill an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:24-25). The record of the kings keeps his name in it: David did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord and turned not aside from any thing that He commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1 Kings 15:5). The ancestry of Christ keeps his name in it too: David the king fathered Solomon by the woman who had been the wife of Urias (Matthew 1:6). He was not delivered from the fatal order, and his faithfulness is not measured by whether he escaped it. The account honours the conduct of the servant and condemns the king who exploited it.

You shall not bear false witness against another nor raise a false report.

But Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord, and went not down to his house.
And when they had told David, saying, Uriah went not down unto his house, David said unto Uriah, Camest thou not from thy journey? why then didst thou not go down unto thine house?

And Uriah said unto David, The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? as thou livest, and as thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing.

And Uriah said unto David, The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? as thou livest, and as thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing.
And David said to Uriah, Tarry here to day also, and to morrow I will let thee depart. So Uriah abode in Jerusalem that day, and the morrow.
And when David had called him, he did eat and drink before him; and he made him drunk: and at even he went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord, but went not down to his house.
And it came to pass in the morning, that David wrote a letter to Joab, and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
And he wrote in the letter, saying, Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.
And it came to pass, when Joab observed the city, that he assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men were.
And the men of the city went out, and fought with Joab: and there fell some of the people of the servants of David; and Uriah the Hittite died also.

Then David said unto the messenger, Thus shalt thou say unto Joab, Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another: make thy battle more strong against the city, and overthrow it: and encourage thou him.

Who smote Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? did not a woman cast a piece of a millstone upon him from the wall, that he died in Thebez? why went ye nigh the wall? then say thou, Thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.
So the messenger went, and came and shewed David all that Joab had sent him for.
And the messenger said unto David, Surely the men prevailed against us, and came out unto us into the field, and we were upon them even unto the entering of the gate.
And the shooters shot from off the wall upon thy servants; and some of the king’s servants be dead, and thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.
